In mathematics, the '''Thurston norm''' is a function on the second [[homology group]] of an oriented [[3-manifold]] introduced by [[William Thurston]], which measures in a natural way the topological complexity of homology classes represented by surfaces.

==Definition==

Let <math>M</math> be a [[differentiable manifold]] and <math>c \in H_2(M)</math>. Then <math>c</math> can be represented by a smooth [[embedding]] <math>S \to M</math>, where <math>S</math> is a (not necessarily connected) [[Surface (topology)|surface]] that is [[Compact space|compact]] and without boundary. The Thurston norm of <math>c</math> is then defined to be{{sfn|Thurston|1986}}

:<math>\|c\|_T = \min_{S} \sum_{i=1}^n \chi_-(S_i)</math>,

where the minimum is taken over all embedded surfaces <math>S = \bigcup_i S_i</math> (the <math>S_i</math> being the connected components) representing <math>c</math> as above, and <math>\chi_-(F) = \max(0, -\chi(F))</math> is the absolute value of the [[Euler characteristic]] for surfaces which are not spheres (and 0 for spheres).

This function satisfies the following properties:

*<math>\| kc \|_T = |k| \cdot \| c \|_T</math> for <math>c \in H_2(M), k \in \Z</math>;
*<math> \| c_1 + c_2 \|_T \le \| c_1 \|_T + \| c_2 \|_T</math> for <math> c_1, c_2 \in H_2(M) </math>.

These properties imply that <math>\| \cdot \|</math> extends to a function on <math>H_2(M, \Q)</math> which can then be extended by continuity to a [[Norm (mathematics)|seminorm]] <math>\| \cdot \|_T </math> on <math>H_2(M,\R)</math>.{{sfn|Thurston|1986|loc=Theorem 1}} By [[Poincaré duality]], one can define the Thurston norm on <math>H^1(M, \R)</math>.

When <math>M</math> is compact with boundary, the Thurston norm is defined in a similar manner on the [[relative homology]] group <math>H_2(M, \partial M, \R)</math> and its Poincaré dual <math>H^1(M,\R)</math>.

It follows from further work of [[David Gabai]]{{sfn|Gabai|1983}} that one can also define the Thurston norm using only [[Immersion (mathematics)|immersed]] surfaces. This implies that the Thurston norm is also equal to half the [[Gromov norm]] on homology.

== Topological applications ==

The Thurston norm was introduced in view of its applications to [[fiber bundle|fibering]]s and [[foliation]]s of 3-manifolds.

The unit ball <math>B</math> of the Thurston norm of a 3-manifold <math>M</math> is a [[polytope]] with integer vertices. It can be used to describe the structure of the set of fiberings of <math>M</math> over the circle: if <math>M</math> can be written as the [[mapping torus]] of a diffeomorphism <math>f</math> of a surface <math>S</math> then the embedding <math>S \hookrightarrow M</math> represents a class in a top-dimensional (or open) face of <math>B</math>: moreover all other integer points on the same face are also fibers in such a fibration.{{sfn|Thurston|1986|loc=Theorem 5}}

Embedded surfaces which minimise the Thurston norm in their homology class are exactly the closed leaves of foliations of <math>M</math>.{{sfn|Gabai|1983}}
